text: Turning on MFA for an entire organization in one flip looks simple on paper, but it almost never is. Engineering a real rollout means staging the risk across phases instead of eliminating a step, so this lesson covers how to group users, plan for exceptions, and handle the communication a rollout actually needs.

A real rollout moves through distinct phases, each one validated before the next expands. The pilot group goes first — IT and security staff who can troubleshoot their own enrollment and surface problems early. High-privilege accounts come next, even though admins often push back the hardest, because their accounts are what an attacker wants most, so protecting them early shrinks real exposure the fastest. General staff follow, department by department, spreading out support load instead of concentrating it in one day. Everyone remaining is enforced last, once earlier phases have worked out the kinks.

Every rollout runs into the same exceptions, and planning for them up front beats discovering them mid-rollout. Shared or kiosk devices — a warehouse terminal, a shared nursing-station desk — often need a device-bound factor instead of a personal phone. Service accounts can't tap a phone at all; they need a different authentication model entirely, covered in Lesson 8. Legacy applications that were never built for MFA need a deliberate exception or a scheduled replacement. Break-glass accounts — a small set of emergency credentials kept outside normal enforcement — need to exist, stay few, and be monitored closely.

Exceptions should be explicit, narrow, and watched, never silent. A policy that requires MFA for all users still names its specific exclusions by account, and pairs every exclusion with monitoring that alerts on any sign-in from that account, so a break-glass or legacy-app carve-out never quietly becomes a permanent, unwatched gap.

Next, Lesson 7 looks at why FIDO2 and passkeys are considered stronger than the SMS and push-based MFA this lesson assumes — public-key credentials bound to the real site's domain resist phishing and the push-fatigue attacks that plague simpler methods.
